note: General houseplant guidance authored for GrowLog. Needs human review before release.

symptom.label: Hard brown bumps on stems or leaves
White or grey crust on soil or pot

context.label: Soil is bone dry for long periods
Soil is hard or water runs straight through
Roots circle the pot or poke out the holes
Near a heater or very hot spot
Not fed for six months or more
Moved to a new spot recently

problems.name: Overwatering
problems.what: The soil stays wet so roots cannot get enough air.
problems.check: Push a finger 3 to 5 cm into the soil. If it is still wet, wait before watering.
steps: Stop watering until the top few centimetres are dry.
Make sure water can drain out of the pot and empty the saucer.
If the soil is soggy all through, move the plant to a bright spot with airflow so it dries faster.
problems.prevent: Water only when the top of the soil is dry to the touch, and use a pot with a drainage hole.
problems.worry: If the base turns soft or smells bad, treat it as root rot.

problems.name: Underwatering
problems.what: The plant is not getting enough water for its needs.
problems.check: Lift the pot: a light pot and dry soil far down mean it is thirsty.
steps: Water slowly until it drains from the bottom, then empty the saucer.
If the soil has shrunk from the pot edge, bottom-water the pot for 20 to 30 minutes.
Check again in a few days and set a regular rhythm.
problems.prevent: Check the soil on a schedule and water thoroughly rather than with small sips.
problems.worry: If leaves stay crisp after a few weeks of regular watering, the roots may be damaged.

problems.name: Inconsistent watering
problems.what: Swings between too wet and too dry stress the roots.
problems.check: Think back: has the soil gone from soaked to bone dry more than once?
steps: Pick a simple routine: check the soil on the same day each week.
Water thoroughly each time, then let the top dry before the next watering.
Trim badly damaged leaves once the routine is steady.
problems.prevent: Use a soil check, not the calendar alone.
problems.worry: If new leaves keep coming in damaged after a steady routine, look at light and roots.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.what: Roots stay wet, die back and turn soft, so the plant cannot drink.
problems.check: Slide the plant out of its pot. Healthy roots are firm and pale. Rotten roots are brown or black, mushy and smell sour.
steps: Remove the plant and cut away all soft, dark roots with clean scissors.
Repot in fresh, free-draining mix in a clean pot with drainage holes.
Water lightly afterwards and keep it in bright, indirect light.
problems.prevent: Use a well-draining mix and never leave the pot standing in water.
problems.worry: If more than half the roots are gone or the stem base is mushy, the plant may not recover. Take cuttings from healthy stems if you can.

problems.name: Edema (water blisters)
problems.what: Roots take up more water than leaves can release, so cells swell into small bumps.
problems.check: Look under the leaves for small blister-like bumps that may turn brown and corky.
steps: Water less often and let the soil dry a bit more between waterings.
Give the plant more light and airflow.
Do not remove leaves unless they are fully damaged. Existing bumps will not heal.
problems.prevent: Avoid watering when the air is cool and humid, and keep the plant in good light.
problems.worry: If you see bumps plus soft stems or leaves, check the roots for rot.

problems.name: Tap-water mineral or chlorine burn
problems.what: Salts or chlorine in tap water build up and scorch leaf tips.
problems.check: Check for white crust on the soil or pot rim and brown, dry tips.
steps: Let tap water sit out overnight before using it, or use rainwater or filtered water.
Flush the soil with plenty of water every few months so salts drain out.
Trim brown tips with clean scissors if you like. They will not turn green again.
problems.prevent: Use soft water where you can, and flush the pot occasionally.
problems.worry: If damage keeps spreading, check humidity and feeding too.

problems.name: Low humidity
problems.what: Dry air pulls moisture from leaf edges faster than the plant can replace it.
problems.check: Brown, crispy tips on several leaves, especially in winter with heating, point to dry air.
steps: Move the plant away from heaters, vents and drafts.
Group plants together or use a humidifier.
Keep watering steady. Misting helps very little and can cause leaf spots.
problems.prevent: Keep humidity-loving plants away from radiators and air conditioners.
problems.worry: If the whole plant crisps despite steady care, check for pests such as spider mites.

problems.name: Too little light
problems.what: The plant is stretching and slowing down because it is not getting enough light.
problems.check: Compare new growth with older growth. Long gaps between leaves and small, pale new leaves point to low light.
steps: Move the plant to a brighter spot, ideally near a window with indirect light.
Rotate the pot every week or two for even growth.
Cut back long, bare stems to encourage fuller growth in spring.
problems.prevent: Match the plant to the light in your room, or add a grow light.
problems.worry: If the plant keeps declining in a bright spot, look at watering and roots.

problems.name: Too much direct light (sunburn)
problems.what: Strong sun scorches leaf tissue and leaves pale or brown patches.
problems.check: The damage sits on the side facing the window, and it is crisp or bleached.
steps: Move the plant back from the window or filter the light with a sheer curtain.
Do not cut healthy leaves. Trim only badly burned ones.
Raise light slowly if you want to move it into more sun.
problems.prevent: Introduce more light gradually over a week or two.
problems.worry: If new leaves also burn, the spot is too intense and the plant should move.

problems.name: Sudden light change
problems.what: A move to a very different spot makes plants drop or yellow leaves while they adjust.
problems.check: Did the plant recently move to a different room, window or season of light?
steps: Keep it in its new spot and avoid moving it again for a few weeks.
Keep watering steady.
Expect some leaf loss while it adjusts.
problems.prevent: Move plants gradually when you can.
problems.worry: If decline continues after four to six weeks, check the other causes.

problems.name: Cold or draft damage
problems.what: Cold air makes leaf cells collapse, leaving dark, wet-looking patches.
problems.check: Check if the plant sits against a cold window, near a door, or in a draft.
steps: Move it away from cold glass and drafts.
Keep it above about 12 to 15 °C unless it is a cool-loving plant.
Trim badly damaged leaves.
problems.prevent: Keep tropical houseplants warm and away from open windows in cold weather.
problems.worry: If the stem turns soft or black, treat it as stem rot.

problems.name: Heat stress
problems.what: High temperatures dry the plant out and cause drooping and scorching.
problems.check: Check whether the plant sits near a heater, radiator or hot windowsill.
steps: Move it to a cooler, shaded spot.
Check the soil and water if dry.
Keep it away from hot vents.
problems.prevent: Avoid very hot spots and give plants some breathing room from windows in summer.
problems.worry: If leaves stay crisp after moving, check for pests and roots.

problems.name: Nitrogen shortage
problems.what: The plant is short of nitrogen, so older leaves pale as it moves nutrients to new growth.
problems.check: Look for older leaves yellowing evenly, with slow growth and a long time since feeding.
steps: Feed with a balanced houseplant fertiliser at half the label strength.
Feed only during the growing season, usually spring and summer.
Do not feed a dry or stressed plant. Water first.
problems.prevent: Feed on a regular schedule during growth, at a gentle dose.
problems.worry: If yellowing continues after a couple of feeds, check roots, light and watering.

problems.name: Magnesium shortage
problems.what: Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
problems.check: Check older leaves for green veins with yellow between them.
steps: Feed with a balanced fertiliser that includes micronutrients, at half strength.
Check that watering and drainage are normal. Roots in poor shape cannot take up nutrients.
Do not add Epsom salt unless you know magnesium is the problem.
problems.prevent: Use a complete fertiliser during the growing season.
problems.worry: If it spreads to many leaves quickly, check roots and watering.

problems.name: Iron shortage
problems.what: New leaves turn yellow between green veins because iron is not available to the plant.
problems.check: Check new leaves for yellow tissue with green veins.
steps: Use a fertiliser with chelated iron at the label dose.
Make sure the soil is not waterlogged, because wet roots block iron uptake.
Use softer water if your tap water is very hard.
problems.prevent: Avoid overwatering and very hard water.
problems.worry: If new leaves stay yellow after correcting watering and feeding, check roots.

problems.name: Fertiliser burn
problems.what: Too much fertiliser leaves salts that burn roots and leaf edges.
problems.check: Look for a white crust on the soil and brown, crisp edges soon after feeding.
steps: Flush the pot with plenty of water, letting it drain fully, three or four times.
Stop feeding for at least two months.
Remove the top crust of soil and replace with fresh mix if heavy.
problems.prevent: Feed at half strength, only in the growing season, and only into moist soil.
problems.worry: If roots look dark and mushy after flushing, check for root damage.

problems.name: Root-bound plant
problems.what: Roots have filled the pot and cannot take up enough water or nutrients.
problems.check: Slide the plant out of the pot. A dense mat of roots circling the outside means it is root-bound.
steps: Repot into a pot one size larger (2 to 5 cm wider) with fresh potting mix.
Loosen the outer roots gently before repotting.
Water well afterwards and keep out of strong sun for a week.
problems.prevent: Repot every year or two in spring, depending on growth.
problems.worry: If the plant is in poor shape after repotting, check roots for rot.

problems.name: Compacted soil
problems.what: Old or heavy soil packs down, so water pools or runs straight past the roots.
problems.check: Water the plant and watch. If water pools on top or rushes out the bottom, the soil is compacted.
steps: Gently loosen the top of the soil with a chopstick.
Repot into fresh, airy potting mix with perlite or bark.
Water slowly in stages so it can soak in.
problems.prevent: Refresh the mix every year or two.
problems.worry: If the plant keeps wilting after repotting, check the roots.

problems.name: Poor drainage
problems.what: Water cannot leave the pot, so roots sit in water.
problems.check: Check that the pot has drainage holes and the saucer is empty.
steps: Move the plant into a pot with drainage holes, or keep it in a nursery pot inside a decorative one.
Use a free-draining mix.
Empty any water from the saucer after watering.
problems.prevent: Always use a pot with drainage holes.
problems.worry: If the soil smells bad or the base is soft, check for root rot.

problems.name: Mineral crust on soil
problems.what: Salts from water and fertiliser build up as a white or grey crust.
problems.check: Look for a hard white or grey crust on the soil or around the pot rim.
steps: Scrape off the crust and replace the top 2 cm of soil.
Flush the pot with water until it runs clear.
Use softer water if you can.
problems.prevent: Flush occasionally and avoid overfeeding.
problems.worry: If leaf tips keep browning, repot into fresh mix.

problems.name: Spider mites
problems.what: Tiny mites suck sap, leaving pale dots and fine webbing.
problems.check: Hold a sheet of white paper under a leaf and tap. Tiny moving specks or webbing mean mites.
steps: Isolate the plant from others.
Wipe leaves, front and back, with a damp cloth, or rinse the plant in the shower.
Spray with a mild soap solution (a few drops of mild liquid soap in a litre of water), test on one leaf first, and repeat every 5 to 7 days for a few weeks.
Raise humidity, since mites thrive in dry air.
problems.prevent: Check leaf undersides regularly and avoid very dry air.
problems.worry: If webbing spreads or leaves yellow and drop quickly, keep treating and keep the plant isolated.

problems.name: Mealybugs
problems.what: Small, soft insects covered in white fluff feed on sap, usually in leaf joints.
problems.check: Look in leaf joints and on stems for white cottony clusters.
steps: Isolate the plant.
Dab each bug with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol (test on one leaf first).
Wipe the plant with a mild soap solution and repeat weekly for several weeks.
problems.prevent: Inspect new plants before bringing them near others.
problems.worry: If they spread to the roots (white fluff in the soil), repot and treat the soil.

problems.name: Scale insects
problems.what: Small, hard bumps on stems and leaves feed on sap and leave sticky residue.
problems.check: Look for brown or tan bumps along stems or leaf veins that you can scrape off with a fingernail.
steps: Isolate the plant.
Scrape or wipe off scales with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Wipe the plant with a mild soap solution and repeat weekly for a few weeks.
problems.prevent: Check stems and leaf undersides when you buy or repot.
problems.worry: If the plant keeps declining, repeat treatment for longer and keep it isolated.

problems.name: Fungus gnats
problems.what: Tiny dark flies lay eggs in constantly damp soil.
problems.check: Notice small dark flies around the soil, especially after watering.
steps: Let the top 3 to 5 cm of soil dry out between waterings.
Use yellow sticky traps to catch adults.
Top the soil with a thin layer of sand or grit.
problems.prevent: Avoid keeping soil constantly wet.
problems.worry: If plants wilt too, check roots for rot.

problems.name: Thrips
problems.what: Slender, tiny insects scrape leaves and leave silvery streaks and distorted growth.
problems.check: Tap a leaf over white paper. Thrips look like tiny dark slivers that move.
steps: Isolate the plant.
Wipe leaves and spray with a mild soap solution.
Repeat every 5 to 7 days for several weeks.
problems.prevent: Inspect new plants and flowers before bringing them in.
problems.worry: If new growth stays distorted after several weeks, keep treating.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.what: Soft insects cluster on new growth and suck sap.
problems.check: Look at soft new shoots and buds for small green, black or brown clusters.
steps: Rinse the plant or wipe off aphids.
Spray with a mild soap solution.
Repeat every few days until they are gone.
problems.prevent: Check soft new growth regularly.
problems.worry: If they return quickly, isolate and keep treating.

problems.name: Whiteflies
problems.what: Tiny white flyers rise up when the plant is disturbed.
problems.check: Shake the plant gently. A cloud of tiny white flies points to whiteflies.
steps: Isolate the plant.
Use yellow sticky traps for adults.
Wipe the leaf undersides and spray with a mild soap solution every 5 to 7 days.
problems.prevent: Check leaf undersides regularly.
problems.worry: If the infestation persists, repeat treatments for several weeks.

problems.name: Chewing pests (caterpillars, slugs, beetles)
problems.what: Larger pests chew holes or ragged edges into leaves.
problems.check: Look under leaves and in the soil, ideally in the evening, for caterpillars, slugs, snails or beetles. Slime trails are a clue.
steps: Pick pests off by hand and move them away from the plant.
Check nearby plants, especially ones outdoors or recently brought in.
Remove badly damaged leaves.
problems.prevent: Check plants you move outdoors, and inspect them before bringing them back in.
problems.worry: If damage continues after you have removed the pests you can see, check again after dark.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.what: A fungus forms a white powdery coating on leaves.
problems.check: The powder can be wiped off and appears on the upper leaf surface.
steps: Isolate the plant.
Remove badly affected leaves.
Improve airflow and keep leaves dry.
Spray with a mix of 1 teaspoon baking soda in a litre of water (test on one leaf), or use a product labelled for powdery mildew.
problems.prevent: Give plants space and avoid wetting the leaves.
problems.worry: If it keeps returning, treat the plant longer and reduce humidity.

problems.name: Fungal leaf spot
problems.what: Fungi cause brown or black spots, often with a darker ring or yellow halo.
problems.check: Check whether spots have clear edges or a yellow halo and appear after wet leaves.
steps: Remove badly spotted leaves.
Avoid wetting the leaves and improve airflow.
Do not water in the evening.
problems.prevent: Water at the soil, not the leaves.
problems.worry: If spots spread to new leaves quickly, keep treating and isolate the plant.

problems.name: Bacterial leaf spot
problems.what: Water-soaked, angular spots with yellow halos are a sign of bacterial infection.
problems.check: Look for spots that look wet or greasy and are limited by the veins.
steps: Remove affected leaves and throw them away, not in compost.
Keep leaves dry and wash your hands and tools afterwards.
Isolate the plant.
problems.prevent: Water at the soil and avoid splashing.
problems.worry: If it spreads fast, consider discarding the plant to protect others.

problems.name: Grey mould (botrytis)
problems.what: A grey, fuzzy mould grows on dead or damaged tissue in damp, still air.
problems.check: Look for grey fuzz on flowers, dead leaves or stems.
steps: Remove affected parts and discard them.
Increase airflow and reduce humidity.
Remove dead leaves and flowers regularly.
problems.prevent: Clear dead material and give the plant air.
problems.worry: If it spreads onto healthy stems, isolate the plant.

problems.name: Rust
problems.what: A fungus causes orange or rust-coloured powdery spots, often under leaves.
problems.check: Rub a spot lightly. Orange powder on your finger suggests rust.
steps: Remove affected leaves.
Keep leaves dry and improve airflow.
Isolate the plant.
problems.prevent: Water at the soil and keep leaves dry.
problems.worry: If it keeps spreading, keep treating and isolate the plant.

problems.name: Anthracnose
problems.what: A fungal disease causing dark, sunken spots and dry browning from the tips and edges.
problems.check: Look for dark, slightly sunken spots with a margin, and browning that spreads from the edges.
steps: Remove affected leaves.
Keep leaves dry and improve airflow.
Do not crowd plants.
problems.prevent: Avoid wetting the leaves and give plants space.
problems.worry: If it spreads, isolate the plant.

problems.name: Stem rot
problems.what: The base or stem turns soft and dark, often from wet, cold conditions.
problems.check: Gently press the base of the stem. If it is soft, mushy or black, it is rotting.
steps: Cut above the rot into healthy green tissue with clean scissors.
Root healthy cuttings in water or fresh mix if you can.
Discard the rotten parts and clean the pot before reuse.
problems.prevent: Do not overwater and avoid cold, wet conditions.
problems.worry: If rot reaches the main stem, the plant may not survive. Save cuttings.

problems.name: Sooty mould
problems.what: A black film grows on sticky honeydew left by sap-sucking insects.
problems.check: Wipe a leaf with a damp cloth. If the black film wipes off and the leaf is sticky, it is sooty mould.
steps: Wipe the film off with a damp cloth.
Look for the pests that made the honeydew, such as aphids, scale or mealybugs, and treat them.
Keep the leaves clean.
problems.prevent: Treat the pests first. The mould follows them.
problems.worry: If the film returns, there are still pests present.

problems.name: Normal older leaf drop
problems.what: Plants shed their oldest leaves over time.
problems.check: Is it only a leaf or two at the bottom, while the rest of the plant looks healthy?
steps: No action is needed. Remove fallen leaves to keep things tidy.
Keep your normal care routine.
problems.prevent: Nothing to prevent. This is part of growth.
problems.worry: If many leaves drop at once, check watering and light.

problems.name: Winter dormancy
problems.what: Many plants slow or pause growth when days are short and cool.
problems.check: Is it winter, and is the plant otherwise healthy?
steps: Water less often and pause feeding.
Keep the plant in its brightest spot.
Resume normal care in spring.
problems.prevent: Reduce watering and feeding in the cool season.
problems.worry: If leaves yellow or soften, check for overwatering.

problems.name: Repotting shock
problems.what: Disturbed roots need a few weeks to recover, so leaves can droop or drop.
problems.check: Was the plant repotted in the last month?
steps: Keep the soil lightly moist, not wet.
Keep the plant out of direct sun for a couple of weeks.
Do not feed for about a month.
problems.prevent: Handle roots gently and repot in the growing season.
problems.worry: If it keeps declining after six weeks, check roots for rot.

problems.name: Settling in after purchase
problems.what: A new home means different light, humidity and temperature, so plants often drop or yellow a few leaves.
problems.check: Was the plant bought or moved in the last few weeks?
steps: Place it in a stable spot with suitable light and leave it.
Water only when the soil is dry.
Avoid repotting or feeding for a few weeks.
problems.prevent: Give new plants a stable spot and a few weeks to adjust.
problems.worry: If decline continues past a month, check for pests and watering.

problems.name: Natural flower fade
problems.what: Flowers wither and brown as they finish, which is natural.
problems.check: Did the plant recently finish flowering?
steps: Remove spent flowers and flower stalks.
Keep your normal care routine.
Some plants rest briefly after flowering.
problems.prevent: Nothing to prevent.
problems.worry: If leaves also yellow or drop, check watering and light.
